extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, students and scholars of literature/poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic poetry/drama (Aristotelian Poetics): what a tragedy is, its essential parts, structural requirements, devices, and the proper use of language, music, and spectacle to produce catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; effected by means of language embellished with each of the kinds of artistic ornament (rhythm, harmony, and metre) and enacted rather than narrated; its proper effect is to arouse pity and fear and thereby to effect a catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components to check: seriousness (not trivial subject), completeness/wholeness (a whole action), magnitude (suitable scope/size), use of language with rhythm/harmony/metre, enactment (drama rather than mere narration), and emotional outcome (pity and fear leading to catharsis). Example phrasing on the page: 'Imitatio Actionis seriæ & perfectæ... purgans [pity and fear]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is composed of six parts: Plot (fabula or constitution of incidents), Character (mores), Thought (sententiae), Diction (dictio / elocution), Song/Melody (modulatio / music), and Spectacle/Apparatus (visual staging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six are the required dimensions for evaluating a tragedy; the text states them explicitly and notes their relative importance (plot first, then character, etc.). Use them as a checklist when analyzing or constructing a tragedy. Quoted list: 'Fabula, Mores, Dictio, Sententiæ, Apparatus, & Modulatio.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Fabula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the arrangement of incidents; the constitution of the action) is the soul of tragedy and is primary: tragedy imitates actions, not merely characters; the end (plot) matters more than moral depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the action has causal unity, a coherent beginning, middle, and end, and whether the incidents fit together to form a whole. Avoid episodes that are mere sequences without causal necessity. The page emphasizes that 'Fabula eſt Principe & quaſi anima Tragediæ.' Use of devices such as peripeteia and anagnorisis belongs to plot (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and totality (beginning, middle, end; magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be a whole possessing magnitude: it must have a beginning, a middle, and an end (principium, medium, finis) so that the sequence of events follows a natural causal order and attains a complete whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the play's structure is not disjointed: the beginning should not depend on something preceding it, the middle should arise from the beginning and lead to the end, and the end should follow from what comes before. Magnitude means appropriate scope—large enough to be complete but not diffuse. The text: 'Totum... habet principium, medium & finem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and anagnorisis (reversal & recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals of fortune (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis) are important plot devices that produce pleasure and contribute strongly to the tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plots where reversals and recognitions arise naturally from the action and are causally linked rather than contrived. Aristotle notes these parts 'maxime oblectatur' (delight the soul) and are key to effective plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Mores) — quality and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are the agents of action and must be portrayed as having certain moral qualities (better, worse, or similar to average); character is the second element after plot and should be appropriate, consistent, and suitable to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters' moral make-up fits and motivates the action, whether they behave consistently, and whether their dispositions serve the plot. The text contrasts imitation of better vs worse people as appropriate to different genres (tragic imitation tends toward better or nobler actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought / Sententia (ideas, themes, reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (sententia) is the faculty of saying what is fitting — the themes, arguments, propositions, and insights expressed in speech; it shows the intellectual aspect of the characters and the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the clarity and aptness of the play's ideas and the capacity of dialogue/monologue to express judgments and principles. Thought occupies a distinct role (after plot and character) in producing persuasive, meaningful drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (Dictio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the apt choice and arrangement of words and phrases (elocution); it applies in metre and in prose and is the vehicle through which the play's language is realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the appropriateness, clarity, and aesthetic quality of expression, including the fit between language and metre. The page notes diction as 'sermonum' and stresses its role both in metrical composition and in spoken speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song / Melody / Modulation (Modulatio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody or musical element (choral song, modulation) is a highly pleasurable part of tragedy tied to rhythm and harmony; it contributes strongly to the work's aesthetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the effectiveness and integration of musical elements (chorus, song, rhythm) in underpinning mood and enhancing emotional response. Aristotle places modulation among the five parts and calls it 'jucundissima' (most delightful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Apparatus (visual staging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (the visual apparatus: scenery, costumes, stage effects) moves the audience but is the least artistic element of tragedy and depends more on stagecraft than on poetical art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While spectacle can powerfully affect audiences, don't rely on it to substitute for strong plot and character; it is 'artis autem maxime expers' (least proper to the poet). Evaluate whether spectacle supports rather than masks weaknesses in the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes/mediums of imitation and meter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is effected through different means (rhythm, harmony, metre, and language) and manners (narration vs direct personation/representation). Meter choices help determine genre: e.g., hexameter suits epic, iambic and tetrameter suit comic/satyric forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen medium and meter suit the genre and intended effect; mixing meters is possible but constrained ('homer's use of different metres...'); consider whether imitation is done through narration or enactment and which is more effective for the work's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions and what each should imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic/dramatic genres imitate different objects or different levels of people: epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic, and satyrical forms each have distinguishing methods and objects (e.g., comedy often imitates the worse or ridiculous; tragedy the better or noble; epic uses narrative meter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing, ensure the work adheres to the expectations of its genre (tone, subject-matter, metre, and mode of imitation). The text provides historical and formal examples (Homer, Sophocles, Aristophanes, etc.) indicating appropriate forms and origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional effect — pity, fear, and catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: A central criterion is whether the tragedy arouses pity and fear in the audience and achieves catharsis (a purging or purification) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just whether the emotions are elicited but whether they are properly directed by the plot and resolved to produce catharsis. The definition of tragedy centers this emotional outcome as part of the work's purpose.
